extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature and humor theory; writers, playwrights, and comedians studying comic principles
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the essential conditions and techniques that make words, situations, and characters comic — identifying mechanisms (transposition, exaggeration, automatism, gesture vs action, unsociability, etc.) and how a humorist or playwright elicits laughter without arousing emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition between extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect arises from transposing between extreme comparative terms (the very large and the very small, the best and the worst), either from solemn to trivial or the inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both directions are comic; narrowing the interval produces subtler varieties. The transposition may refer to physical dimensions or moral value. Examples and further subdivisions (exaggeration, degradation, mock-heroic) follow from this general principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (physical transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of small things as though they were large is to exaggerate; prolonged and systematic exaggeration is always comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration is a striking form of transposition and has given rise to devices like the mock-heroic poem; methodical braggadocio often produces a mock-heroic aspect that makes us laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward transposition of moral value (respectable language for disreputable ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing scandalous situations, low-class callings, or disgraceful behaviour in terms of the utmost 'respectability' produces comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often succinct (a single word can suffice) because it reveals an accepted system of transposition in social circles and 'a moral organisation of immorality' (example: Gogol — 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank'). Not dependent on length; can be very brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of real and ideal: irony vs humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrast between what is and what ought to be yields irony when we state the ought as actual, and humour when we describe what is and pretend it ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is 'oratorical' while humour is 'scientific' — humour delights in concrete terms, technical details and definite facts; humour may be seen as a transposition from the moral to the scientific (a moralist disguised as a scientist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition into professional/business jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating everyday life or social relations into technical vocabulary or business phraseology produces comic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying a profession's technical terms to ordinary matters (or using commercial formulas in personal relations) can be deeply comic and may reveal character faults (examples: Labiche; scenes where marriage is treated as a business affair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language rigidity and ready-made/formulaic speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Language becomes comic when it is stereotyped, ready-made, mechanical — in contrast to supple, ever-changing, living language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter singles out 'the rigid, the ready-made, the mechanical' as defects. Mechanical operations of inversion and transposition applied to language expose automatism and produce comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsociability / lack of adaptability to society
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who goes his own way without adapting to or being attentive to social surroundings (unsociability) is comic; comedy expresses a lack of adaptability to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions socially as a kind of correction or 'ragging' — it humiliates to encourage conformity. Examples: the socially withdrawn honest man (Alceste) becomes ludicrous because of unsociability rather than immorality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional neutrality of the audience (appeal to intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy (and laughter) appeals to intelligence and is incompatible with aroused emotion; if sympathy, fear, or pity are stirred, laughter is prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To render even odious vices laughable, the comic poet must prevent emotions from being moved. The sole necessary condition for making something potentially ludicrous is that it must not arouse the spectator's feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of feeling (parasitic feeling / rigidity within the soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: A feeling depicted as isolated, a 'parasitic organism' with an independent existence inside the character's soul, prevents emotional contagion and yields comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an intense feeling does not impregnate other mental states (remains rigid and isolated), it alienates sympathy and appears puppet-like, provoking laughter (example: Harpagon's greed passes by other feelings absentmindedly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gesture rather than action
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy directs attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, even automatic language) rather than to deliberate actions; gesture is automatic, action is intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesture 'slips out unawares' and can jolt the audience out of emotional engagement; when attention is fixed on gesture instead of action, we enter the realm of comedy (example: Tartuffe's material sincerity and gestures render him comic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / absentmindedness / unconscious contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically — involuntary gestures, unconscious remarks, systematic absentmindedness reveal the comic in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profoundly comic characters show aspects of themselves they are unaware of (contradicting their words with actions). Systematic absentmindedness (Don Quixote) is among the most comical things imaginable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as general types / stock characters
rubrics_metrics.description: High-class comedy aims to depict general types; every comic character is a type and comedy seeks the general rather than the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becoming like a ready-made category (a stock character) is comic; comedy's subject-matter is generality and this distinguishes it from tragedy and drama where characters and situations are welded together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of rigidity proportional to comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is proportional to the rigidity of the character or behaviour — the more rigid (automatism, stereotype), the funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the part of personality that appeals to feeling is set aside, the remaining rigid or mechanical element is capable of becoming comic; rigidity, automatism, absentmindedness and unsociability are entwined ingredients of the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to prevent audience sympathy (lulling sensibility / dampening emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic poet employs methods to keep the audience's sympathy asleep or to 'throw a wet blanket' on feeling so that serious situations are not taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods are noted: isolating the feeling within the character (making it parasitic) and using devices that dampen or block sympathy, thereby allowing potentially serious material to become comic.
